triage.name: Membranous nephropathy
triage.reason: Adult nephrotic syndrome with edema and heavy proteinuria; biopsy-based diagnosis with secondary causes and other nephrotic syndromes as look-alikes.

demographics: More common in adults than children
Slightly more common in men than women
In adults, primary membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome
In children, membranous nephropathy is rare and usually secondary to another condition

risk_factors.text: Autoimmune disease such as systemic lupus erythematosus
Chronic hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection
Use of certain medications such as NSAIDs or penicillamine
Exposure to heavy metals or industrial solvents

family_history: Autoimmune disease in a first-degree relative
exposures: Heavy metals such as mercury or gold

chief_complaints.text: My ankles and legs are swollen
I feel puffy around my eyes in the morning
I've gained weight without eating more

hpi.duration: Usually weeks to months before presentation
hpi.progression: Swelling starts in the ankles and legs, then may spread to the abdomen and face; fatigue and foamy urine develop as protein loss continues
hpi.location: Lower extremities, periorbital area, and abdomen
hpi.quality: Pitting swelling that is worse in the evening and after standing
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate at first, becoming uncomfortable and limiting activity as it progresses
hpi.timing: Worse in the evening and after prolonged standing; periorbital swelling is worst in the morning

associated_symptoms.text: Puffiness around the eyes in the morning

pertinent_negatives: Recent sore throat or skin infection

positives.text: Swelling of the ankles and legs

negatives: Blood clots in the legs or lungs

atypical.how_it_differs: Membranous nephropathy is rare in children; when it occurs it is usually secondary to another condition such as hepatitis B or autoimmune disease, and may present with isolated proteinuria rather than obvious edema.
More likely to be secondary to a malignancy or medication, and may present with less edema and more nonspecific fatigue or weight loss.
Edema and proteinuria can be attributed to preeclampsia; membranous nephropathy is a rare cause and usually diagnosed before pregnancy or after persistent proteinuria postpartum.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable at rest, mild ankle swelling noted on inspection
general.moderate: Puffy face and swollen legs, moves slowly, clothes or shoes feel tight
general.severe: Markedly edematous, dyspneic on exertion, uncomfortable lying flat
general.critical: Anasarca with respiratory distress, ill-appearing, may be hypotensive or oliguric

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the dorsum of the foot or the medial malleolus for several seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities, graded 1+ to 4+

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face and periorbital area in the morning or after lying flat
Record the patient's weight and compare with prior weights
findings.finding: Recent weight gain from fluid retention

findings.maneuver: Percuss the flanks for dullness and test for shifting dullness or a fluid wave
Percuss and auscultate the lung bases
findings.finding: Dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds at the bases

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms with an appropriately sized cuff
Inspect the internal jugular vein at 45 degrees
Auscultate the heart at the apex with the bell
Inspect the face and sun-exposed skin
Inspect and palpate the small joints of the hands, wrists and knees
Palpate the cervical, axillary and inguinal lymph node chains

labs.caveat: Dipstick protein is a screening result; quantify with a 24-hour urine protein or spot protein-to-creatinine ratio.
Microscopic hematuria can occur but is not typical; prominent hematuria with red cell casts suggests another glomerulonephritis.
Hyaline and granular casts are nonspecific; red cell casts point away from membranous nephropathy.
Hypoalbuminemia reflects urinary protein loss; values below 2.5 g/dL mark severe nephrotic syndrome.
Low total protein follows albumin loss.
Hyperlipidemia is part of the nephrotic syndrome and contributes to cardiovascular risk.
Many patients have normal kidney function at diagnosis; a rising creatinine suggests progressive disease or a superimposed process.
Mild normocytic anemia can occur with chronic kidney disease or from urinary loss of transferrin and erythropoietin deficiency.
Reactive thrombocytosis can accompany the nephrotic state and adds to thrombotic risk.
Elevated fibrinogen and other clotting factors contribute to the hypercoagulable state.
Can be elevated from the nephrotic state itself; order only when thrombosis is suspected.
Not routine; consider only if adrenal insufficiency is a competing diagnosis.

imaging.preferred_when: Initial evaluation of nephrotic-range proteinuria to assess kidney size and rule out obstruction or structural disease

findings.text: Small, shrunken kidneys suggesting chronic irreversible disease

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Search for occult malignancy in older adults with unexplained secondary membranous nephropathy

findings.text: Solid organ mass or lymphadenopathy suggesting an underlying malignancy

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected renal vein thrombosis (flank pain, hematuria, sudden decline in kidney function)

findings.text: Absent or reduced flow in the renal vein

Assesses kidney function, electrolytes and acid-base status
Provides albumin and total protein to confirm hypoalbuminemia and gauge severity

Looks for anemia, thrombocytosis and other cytopenias
Confirms two kidneys, assesses size and echogenicity, and rules out obstruction
Quantifies proteinuria when a 24-hour collection is impractical
Quantifies protein excretion and establishes nephrotic-range proteinuria
Required before immunosuppressive therapy or biopsy in anyone who could be pregnant
initial.only_if: patient is a woman of childbearing potential

confirmatory.test: Kidney biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy
confirmatory.why: Definitive diagnosis; shows subepithelial immune deposits and basement membrane thickening
Serologic marker of primary membranous nephropathy; positive results can support the diagnosis and guide monitoring

supporting.why: Nonspecific marker of inflammation or underlying systemic disease
Helps identify an inflammatory or infectious process
Thyroid disease can be associated with membranous nephropathy and with edema
Identifies diabetes, which can cause nephrotic-range proteinuria and affect management

supporting.test: Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody
supporting.why: Chronic hepatitis B is a treatable secondary cause
Chronic hepatitis C is a treatable secondary cause
HIV-associated nephropathy and immune complex disease can mimic membranous nephropathy
Screens for systemic lupus erythematosus, a common secondary cause
Supports lupus nephritis when ANA is positive
Low complement suggests lupus or another immune complex process rather than primary membranous nephropathy

supporting.test: Serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains
supporting.why: Screens for monoclonal gammopathy or plasma cell dyscrasia in older adults

supporting.why: Searches for occult solid tumor in older adults with unexplained membranous nephropathy

decision_points: Confirm nephrotic-range proteinuria before proceeding to kidney biopsy
Check PLA2R antibody; a positive result supports primary membranous nephropathy and may avoid biopsy in some patients
Screen for secondary causes (lupus, hepatitis B and C, HIV, malignancy, medications) before labeling the disease primary
Assess thrombotic risk; nephrotic syndrome with albumin below 2.5 g/dL carries a higher risk of renal vein thrombosis
Hold or adjust immunosuppressive planning until infection and malignancy are excluded

criteria.name: Nephrotic syndrome
criteria.summary: Nephrotic-range proteinuria (generally more than 3.5 g per day) with hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia.
items: Proteinuria greater than 3.5 g per 24 hours

criteria.name: Membranous nephropathy (biopsy)
criteria.summary: Kidney biopsy shows subepithelial immune deposits along the glomerular basement membrane with basement membrane thickening and spike formation on silver stain.
items: Light microscopy: diffusely thickened glomerular basement membrane
Immunofluorescence: granular IgG and C3 along the capillary loops

differential.name: Minimal change disease
differential.why_considered: The other major cause of nephrotic syndrome with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and edema; can look identical at the bedside.
differential.trigger: Sudden-onset nephrotic syndrome, especially in a child or young adult, or after a recent infection or NSAID use

history: Abrupt onset over days to a couple of weeks
Recent upper respiratory infection or allergic reaction
Recent NSAID use
exam: Marked edema with preserved blood pressure

differential.name: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
differential.why_considered: Common cause of nephrotic-range proteinuria in adults, often with hypertension and slowly declining kidney function.
differential.trigger: Nephrotic proteinuria with hypertension, hematuria or reduced kidney function, especially in an African American patient or with HIV, obesity or prior heroin use

history: More likely to have hypertension and hematuria
HIV infection, obesity, or prior heroin use
Family history of kidney disease in some forms
exam: Edema often less dramatic than in minimal change disease
labs: Higher creatinine for the degree of proteinuria
imaging: Normal or small kidneys on ultrasound

differential.name: Diabetic nephropathy
differential.why_considered: Very common cause of nephrotic-range proteinuria in adults, with edema and hypertension.
differential.trigger: Long-standing diabetes with proteinuria, retinopathy or declining kidney function

history: Diabetes for many years
Progressive proteinuria over years rather than months
Coexisting neuropathy or retinopathy
exam: Findings of diabetic retinopathy on fundoscopy
labs: Proteinuria that is often less selective
imaging: Normal to enlarged kidneys early, smaller later

differential.name: Lupus nephritis
differential.why_considered: Systemic lupus erythematosus can produce nephrotic syndrome and is a common secondary cause of membranous nephropathy.
differential.trigger: Nephrotic syndrome with rash, arthritis, oral ulcers, cytopenias or low complement in a young woman

history: Malar or photosensitive rash
Joint pain and swelling
Oral ulcers, hair loss, Raynaud phenomenon
imaging: No specific renal imaging finding; kidney biopsy shows immune complex deposition

differential.name: Hepatitis B-associated nephropathy
differential.why_considered: Chronic hepatitis B is a well-recognized secondary cause of membranous nephropathy, particularly in children and in endemic areas.

history: Birth in or travel to a high-prevalence region
Injection drug use or high-risk sexual behavior
Known chronic hepatitis B
labs: Low complement levels in some cases
imaging: Hepatic ultrasound showing chronic liver changes

differential.name: Amyloidosis
differential.why_considered: Deposition of amyloid in the glomeruli causes nephrotic-range proteinuria, often with other organ involvement.

history: Older adult with fatigue and weight loss
Macroglossia, carpal tunnel syndrome, or heart failure symptoms
Underlying plasma cell dyscrasia or chronic inflammatory disease
exam: Signs of heart failure or neuropathy
labs: Monoclonal protein on serum or urine protein electrophoresis
Low voltage on ECG if cardiac involvement
imaging: Kidney biopsy with Congo red-positive deposits

differential.name: Preeclampsia
differential.why_considered: Pregnancy causes edema, proteinuria and hypertension that can mimic nephrotic syndrome.
differential.trigger: Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks with new hypertension and proteinuria

history: Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks
Headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain
imaging: Fetal growth restriction on ultrasound in severe cases

severity.mild: Subnephrotic or low-grade nephrotic proteinuria with mild ankle edema, normal kidney function and normal blood pressure
severity.moderate: Full nephrotic syndrome with albumin below 3.0 g/dL, marked edema, hyperlipidemia and preserved kidney function
severity.severe: Nephrotic syndrome with albumin below 2.5 g/dL, anasarca, hypertension, rising creatinine, or a thrombotic complication
severity.critical: Life-threatening complications such as massive pulmonary embolism, renal vein thrombosis with acute kidney injury, severe sepsis, or respiratory failure from anasarca

red_flags.finding: Sudden flank pain with hematuria and a rapid decline in kidney function
red_flags.meaning: Suspected renal vein thrombosis; needs urgent imaging and anticoagulation

red_flags.finding: Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, or hypoxemia
red_flags.meaning: Possible pulmonary embolism; nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state

red_flags.finding: Fever, cough, or focal lung findings
red_flags.meaning: Infection; patients on immunosuppression or with low immunoglobulin are at higher risk
Severe nephrotic syndrome with high thrombotic and infectious risk
Progressive kidney injury, possible crescentic transformation or acute interstitial nephritis

red_flags.finding: Weight loss, night sweats, or a new mass
red_flags.meaning: Possible underlying malignancy causing secondary membranous nephropathy

complications.name: Deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism

special_populations.differences: Membranous nephropathy is rare in children; when it occurs it is usually secondary to hepatitis B or autoimmune disease, and may present with isolated proteinuria rather than obvious edema.
More likely to be secondary to a malignancy or medication; may present with less edema and more nonspecific fatigue or weight loss, and warrants a search for occult cancer.

Edema and proteinuria can be attributed to preeclampsia; membranous nephropathy is a rare cause and is usually diagnosed before pregnancy or after persistent proteinuria postpartum. Management must account for fetal safety of immunosuppressive agents.
Reduced kidney function at diagnosis suggests a more aggressive course or a superimposed process; medication dosing must be adjusted and nephrotoxins avoided.
Higher risk of infection and of secondary causes such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV; immunosuppressive therapy requires careful monitoring.

key_questions.question: When did the swelling start, and how has it changed over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months, starting in the ankles and legs and spreading upward; a sudden onset over days suggests minimal change disease instead

key_questions.question: Does your urine look foamy or frothy?
key_questions.looking_for: Foamy urine, which reflects heavy protein loss into the urine

key_questions.question: Have you gained weight recently without eating more?
key_questions.looking_for: Weight gain from fluid retention, often several pounds over weeks

key_questions.question: Is the swelling worse at any particular time of day?
key_questions.looking_for: Leg swelling worse in the evening and after standing; periorbital puffiness worst in the morning

key_questions.question: Have you noticed blood in your urine, or pain in your flank?
key_questions.looking_for: Usually absent; sudden flank pain with hematuria suggests renal vein thrombosis, a complication of the nephrotic state

key_questions.question: Have you had any fevers, night sweats, or weight loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms raise concern for an underlying malignancy or chronic infection causing secondary membranous nephropathy

key_questions.question: Do you have any joint pain, rash, oral ulcers, or sensitivity to sunlight?
key_questions.looking_for: Features of systemic lupus erythematosus, a common secondary cause

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or HIV?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic viral infection as a treatable secondary cause of membranous nephropathy

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, and if so for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-standing diabetes suggests diabetic nephropathy as a competing cause of nephrotic-range proteinuria

key_questions.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with cancer, or do you have a history of a tumor?
key_questions.looking_for: Solid tumors and lymphomas are associated with secondary membranous nephropathy, especially in older adults

key_questions.question: Have you taken NSAIDs, penicillamine, captopril, or gold therapy?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that can cause secondary membranous nephropathy; stopping the drug may lead to remission

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had kidney disease or an autoimmune disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of autoimmune disease or inherited kidney disease

key_questions.question: Have you had blood clots in your legs or lungs before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior thrombosis; nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state with risk of renal vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Have you noticed shortness of breath, especially with activity or when lying flat?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspnea from pleural effusions or anasarca; orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea would point toward heart failure instead

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy must be excluded before biopsy or immunosuppressive therapy; preeclampsia is a competing cause of edema and proteinuria

reasoning_points: Nephrotic syndrome in an adult: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia
Gradual onset of lower extremity and periorbital edema over weeks to months with foamy urine
Age 40 to 60 with a slight male predominance; primary membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults
Secondary causes considered and excluded: lupus, hepatitis B and C, HIV, solid tumor or lymphoma, and medications such as NSAIDs or penicillamine
PLA2R antibody positive supports primary membranous nephropathy and can guide monitoring
Kidney biopsy is the definitive diagnosis: subepithelial immune deposits, thickened glomerular basement membrane, and granular IgG and C3 on immunofluorescence
Complications of the nephrotic state considered: renal vein thrombosis, venous thromboembolism, infection and progressive kidney disease
Look-alikes distinguished: minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, diabetic nephropathy, lupus nephritis, amyloidosis and preeclampsia

easy: Adult in their 40s or 50s with weeks of progressive leg swelling and foamy urine
Heavy proteinuria on urinalysis with low serum albumin and high cholesterol
No rash, arthritis or other systemic features
Kidney biopsy shows subepithelial deposits and thickened basement membrane
medium: Older adult with nephrotic syndrome and nonspecific fatigue or weight loss, prompting a search for occult malignancy
Patient with known systemic lupus erythematosus presenting with nephrotic-range proteinuria
Patient on long-term NSAIDs or penicillamine who develops proteinuria and edema
Normal kidney function at diagnosis with only mild edema and no hypertension
Microscopic hematuria or mild creatinine elevation that raises focal segmental glomerulosclerosis as an alternative
hard: Nephrotic syndrome with sudden flank pain, hematuria and a rapid decline in kidney function suggesting renal vein thrombosis
Pregnant patient with edema and proteinuria where preeclampsia is the leading concern
Patient with long-standing diabetes where diabetic nephropathy and membranous nephropathy coexist
Older adult with monoclonal gammopathy or heart failure symptoms suggesting amyloidosis
Child with isolated proteinuria and no edema, where membranous nephropathy is rare and usually secondary to hepatitis B
Patient presenting with pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis as the first manifestation of the nephrotic state
